CHAPTER LI

When she came down again she was a changed woman. Her eyes were wet, but
calm, and all her bitterness and excitement charmed away.

“Denys,” said she softly, “I have got my orders. I am to read my lover's
letter to his folk.”

“Ye will never do that?”

“Ay will I.”

“I see there is something in the letter has softened ye towards them.”

“Not a jot, Denys, not a jot. But an I hated them like poison I would
not disobey my love. Denys, 'tis so sweet to obey, and sweetest of all
to obey one who is far, far away, and cannot enforce my duty, but must
trust my love for my obedience. Ah, Gerard, my darling, at hand I might
have slighted thy commands, misliking thy folk as I have cause to do;
but now, didst bid me go into the raging sea and read thy sweet letter
to the sharks, there I'd go. Therefore, Denys, tell his mother I have
got a letter, and if she and hers would hear it, I am their servant; let
them say their hour, and I'll seat them as best I can, and welcome them
as best I may.”

Denys went off to Catherine with this good news. He found the family at
dinner, and told them there was a long letter from Gerard. Then in the
midst of the joy this caused, he said, “And her heart is softened, and
she will read it to you herself; you are to choose your own time.”

“What does she think there are none can read but her?” asked Catherine.
“Let her send the letter and we will read it.”

“Nay, but, mother,” objected little Kate; “mayhap she cannot bear to
part it from her hand; she loves him dearly.”

“What, thinks she we shall steal it?”

Cornelis suggested that she would fain wedge herself into the family by
means of this letter.

Denys cast a look of scorn on the speaker. “There spoke a bad heart,”
 said he. “La camarade hates you all like poison. Oh, mistake me not,
dame; I defend her not, but so 'tis; yet maugre her spleen at a word
from Gerard she proffers to read you his letter with her own pretty
mouth, and hath a voice like honey--sure 'tis a fair proffer.”

“'Tis so, mine honest soldier,” said the father of the family, “and
merits a civil reply, therefore hold your whisht ye that be women, and
I shall answer her. Tell her I, his father, setting aside all past
grudges, do for this grace thank her, and would she have double thanks,
let her send my son's letter by thy faithful hand, the which will I
read to his flesh and blood, and will then to her so surely and faithful
return, as I am Eli a Dierich a William a Luke, free burgher of Tergou,
like my forbears, and like them, a man of my word.”

“Ay, and a man who is better than his word,” cried Catherine; “the only
one I ever did foregather.”

“Hold thy peace, wife.”

“Art a man of sense, Eli, a dirk, a chose, a chose(1),”' shouted Denys.
“The she-comrade will be right glad to obey Gerard and yet not face you
all, whom she hates as wormwood, saving your presence. Bless ye, the
world hath changed, she is all submission to-day: 'obedience is honey,'
quoth she; and in sooth 'tis a sweetmeat she cannot but savour, eating
so little on't, for what with her fair face, and her mellow tongue; and
what wi' flying in fits and terrifying us that be soldiers to death, an
we thwart her; and what wi' chiding us one while, and petting us like
lambs t' other, she hath made two of the crawlingest slaves ever you
saw out of two honest swashbucklers. I be the ironing ruffian, t' other
washes.”

“What next?

“What next? why, whenever the brat is in the world I shall rock cradle,
and t' other knave will wash tucker and bib. So, then, I'll go fetch
the letter on the instant. Ye will let me bide and hear it read, will ye
not?”

“Else our hearts were black as coal,” said Catherine.

So Denys went for the letter. He came back crestfallen. “She will not
let it out of her hand neither to me nor you, nor any he or she that
lives.”

“I knew she would not,” said Cornelis.

“Whisht! whisht!” said Eli, “and let Denys tell his story.”

“'Nay,' said I, 'but be ruled by me.' 'Not I,' quoth she. 'Well, but,'
quoth I, 'that same honey Obedience ye spake of.' 'You are a fool,' says
she; 'obedience to Gerard is sweet, but obedience to any other body, who
ever said that was sweet?'

“At last she seemed to soften a bit, and did give me a written paper for
you, mademoiselle. Here 'tis.”

“For me?” said little Kate, colouring.

“Give that here!” said Eli, and he scanned the writing, and said almost
in a whisper, “These be words from the letter Hearken!

“'And, sweetheart, an if these lines should travel safe to thee, make
thou trial of my people's hearts withal. Maybe they are somewhat turned
towards me, being far away. If 'tis so they will show it to thee, since
now to me they may not. Read, then, this letter! But I do strictly
forbid thee to let it from thy hand; and if they still hold aloof from
thee, why, then say nought, but let them think me dead. Obey me in
this; for, if thou dost disrespect my judgment and my will in this, thou
lovest me not.'”

There was a silence, and Gerard's words copied by Margaret here handed
round and inspected.

“Well,” said Catherine, “that is another matter. But methinks 'tis for
her to come to us, not we to her.”

“Alas, mother! what odds does that make?”

“Much,” said Eli. “Tell her we are over many to come to her, and bid her
hither, the sooner the better.”

When Denys was gone, Eli owned it was a bitter pill to him.

“When that lass shall cross my threshold, all the mischief and misery
she hath made here will seem to come in adoors in one heap. But what
could I do, wife? We must hear the news of Gerard. I saw that in thine
eyes, and felt it in my own heart. And she is backed by our undutiful
but still beloved son, and so is she stronger than we, and brings our
noses down to the grindstone, the sly, cruel jade. But never heed.
We will hear the letter; and then let her go unblessed as she came
unwelcome.”

“Make your mind easy,” said Catherine. “She will not come at all.” And a
tone of regret was visible.

Shortly after Richart, who had been hourly expected, arrived from
Amsterdam grave and dignified in his burgher's robe and gold chain,
ruff, and furred cap, and was received not with affection only, but
respect; for he had risen a step higher than his parents, and such steps
were marked in mediaeval society almost as visibly as those in their
staircases.

Admitted in due course to the family council, he showed plainly, though
not discourteously, that his pride was deeply wounded by their having
deigned to treat with Margaret Brandt. “I see the temptation,” said he.
“But which of us hath not at times to wish one way and do another?” This
threw a considerable chill over the old people. So little Kate put in a
word. “Vex not thyself, dear Richart. Mother says she will not come.

“All the better, sweetheart. I fear me, if she do, I shall hie me back
to Amsterdam.”

Here Denys popped his head in at the door, and said--

“She will be here at three on the great dial.”

They all looked at one another in silence.

     (1) Anglice, a Thing-em-bob.

When she came down again, she was not the same woman who had gone up. The storm in her had spent itself in secret; what returned was quieter, and therefore more perilous. Her eyes still held tears, but the tears lay like clear water in a settled cup—no longer splashing, no longer bitter. Even her mouth, that could twist words into weapons, was softened, as if she had been tasting something sweet and would not waste it.

“Denys,” said she, very low, “I have got my orders. I am to read my lover’s letter to his folk.”

Denys stared, as if she had offered him a dish that looked fair yet smelt of treachery. “Ye will never do that?”

“Ay will I.”

“I see there is something in the letter has softened ye towards them.”

“Not a jot, Denys, not a jot.” Her voice did not rise; it fell, steady as a spoon into honey. “But an I hated them like poison I would not disobey my love. Denys, ’tis so sweet to obey, and sweetest of all to obey one who is far, far away, and cannot enforce my duty, but must trust my love for my obedience.”

As she spoke, the house noises below—footfalls, a chair grating, a pot-lid set down—seemed to come up through the boards and mix with her words, making them homely, almost pious, like grace said over bread.

“Ah, Gerard, my darling,” she murmured, and for an instant she was not addressing Denys at all, but some distance that had a voice of its own. “At hand I might have slighted thy commands, misliking thy folk as I have cause to do; but now, didst bid me go into the raging sea and read thy sweet letter to the sharks, there I’d go. Therefore, Denys, tell his mother I have got a letter, and if she and hers would hear it, I am their servant; let them say their hour, and I’ll seat them as best I can, and welcome them as best I may.”

Denys went off with the message. Downstairs the family sat at dinner: the thick brown bread on the board, the salt near at hand, the steam of the pottage lifting a familiar savour that, in that house, meant safety and custom. The room held also its own music: spoons against earthenware, the quiet chink of knife on trencher, the soft talk that breaks and gathers like a hearth-fire’s crackle.

Denys came in with news that struck straight through all these common sounds as a bell cuts through wind.

“There is a long letter from Gerard.”

Joy leapt like flame in dry straw; even the air seemed to brighten. In the midst of that warmth Denys added, with a soldier’s bluntness made oddly gentle by what he carried, “And her heart is softened, and she will read it to you herself; you are to choose your own time.”

“What does she think there are none can read but her?” Catherine cried at once, setting down her spoon with a sharp click that rang louder than it should in the little room. “Let her send the letter and we will read it.”

“Nay, but, mother,” put in little Kate, and the girl’s cheeks went red, as if the steam from the bowl had found them. “Mayhap she cannot bear to part it from her hand; she loves him dearly.”

“What, thinks she we shall steal it?” said Catherine, with the old suspicion, salted like cured meat.

Cornelis, who had been nursing his own sourness, said, “She would fain wedge herself into the family by means of this letter.”

Denys turned on him with a look like the flat of a blade. “There spoke a bad heart,” said he. “La camarade hates you all like poison. Oh, mistake me not, dame; I defend her not, but so ’tis; yet maugre her spleen at a word from Gerard she proffers to read you his letter with her own pretty mouth, and hath a voice like honey—sure ’tis a fair proffer.”

Eli, Gerard’s father, took the matter as he took the carving-knife: steady, with the wrist set, not without feeling but without flutter. “’Tis so, mine honest soldier,” said he, “and merits a civil reply; therefore hold your whisht, ye that be women, and I shall answer her. Tell her I, his father, setting aside all past grudges, do for this grace thank her; and would she have double thanks, let her send my son’s letter by thy faithful hand, the which will I read to his flesh and blood, and will then to her so surely and faithful return, as I am Eli a Dierich a William a Luke, free burgher of Tergou, like my forbears, and like them, a man of my word.”

“Ay, and a man who is better than his word,” cried Catherine, her sharpness turning all at once to warmth, as if a lump of butter had melted in the pot. “The only one I ever did foregather.”

“Hold thy peace, wife.”

“Art a man of sense, Eli,—a dirk, a chose, a chose,” shouted Denys, in a burst of admiration that made the room laugh in spite of itself. Then, with the gusto of a man tasting his own jest, he ran on: “The she-comrade will be right glad to obey Gerard and yet not face you all, whom she hates as wormwood, saving your presence. Bless ye, the world hath changed; she is all submission to-day: ‘obedience is honey,’ quoth she; and in sooth ’tis a sweetmeat she cannot but savour, eating so little on’t, for what with her fair face and her mellow tongue; and what wi’ flying in fits and terrifying us that be soldiers to death, an we thwart her; and what wi’ chiding us one while, and petting us like lambs t’ other, she hath made two of the crawlingest slaves ever you saw out of two honest swashbucklers. I be the ironing ruffian; t’ other washes.”

“What next?” cried Catherine, half amused, half scandalized.

“What next? Why, whenever the brat is in the world I shall rock cradle, and t’ other knave will wash tucker and bib. So, then, I’ll go fetch the letter on the instant. Ye will let me bide and hear it read, will ye not?”

“Else our hearts were black as coal,” said Catherine.

Denys went out briskly, as if fetching a flagon; and came back as if the flagon had been knocked from his hand. His shoulders drooped; his face wore that crestfallen look soldiers get when a campaign turns on a petty order.

“She will not let it out of her hand neither to me nor you, nor any he or she that lives.”

“I knew she would not,” Cornelis said at once, as if he had been waiting to salt the wound.

“Whisht! whisht!” said Eli. “And let Denys tell his story.”

“‘Nay,’ said I, ‘but be ruled by me.’ ‘Not I,’ quoth she. ‘Well, but,’ quoth I, ‘that same honey Obedience ye spake of.’ ‘You are a fool,’ says she; ‘obedience to Gerard is sweet, but obedience to any other body—who ever said that was sweet?’”

Denys paused, then drew from his pouch a paper folded small, as if it were a spice to be used sparingly. “At last she seemed to soften a bit, and did give me a written paper for you, mademoiselle. Here ’tis.”

“For me?” said little Kate, colouring deeper.

“Give that here!” said Eli, and took it before the girl’s fingers had quite closed. He scanned the writing; his lips moved without sound, tasting the words as if they were unknown meat. Then he spoke, almost in a whisper, for it was as though Gerard’s voice had entered the room and the room must mind its manners.

“These be words from the letter. Hearken!”

And he read:

“‘And, sweetheart, an if these lines should travel safe to thee, make thou trial of my people’s hearts withal. Maybe they are somewhat turned towards me, being far away. If ’tis so they will show it to thee, since now to me they may not. Read, then, this letter! But I do strictly forbid thee to let it from thy hand; and if they still hold aloof from thee, why, then say nought, but let them think me dead. Obey me in this; for, if thou dost disrespect my judgment and my will in this, thou lovest me not.’”

Silence fell—thick, not empty. The very dinner seemed to hold its steam and wait. Those words, copied by Margaret’s hand, went round the table and were looked at as folk look at relics: to be sure the thing is real, to read in the ink the pressure of a mind far off.

“Well,” said Catherine at last, and her tone changed, as when a cook finds the salt must be measured afresh. “That is another matter. But methinks ’tis for her to come to us, not we to her.”

“Alas, mother! what odds does that make?” said little Kate, and in her voice was the young instinct that words are bridges, not walls.

“Much,” said Eli. “Tell her we are over many to come to her, and bid her hither, the sooner the better.”

When Denys was gone again, Eli sat a moment with his hands on the board, as if feeling the grain of it, the old familiar ridges that had known so many meals and so many tidings. “When that lass shall cross my threshold,” said he, “all the mischief and misery she hath made here will seem to come in adoors in one heap. But what could I do, wife? We must hear the news of Gerard. I saw that in thine eyes, and felt it in my own heart. And she is backed by our undutiful but still beloved son, and so is she stronger than we, and brings our noses down to the grindstone, the sly, cruel jade. But never heed. We will hear the letter; and then let her go unblessed as she came unwelcome.”

“Make your mind easy,” said Catherine; but in her there was a small, unwilling ache, like hunger that comes even when pride would rather not eat. “She will not come at all.”

They had scarcely gathered up the board when Richart arrived at last from Amsterdam—grave and set, in his burgher’s robe and gold chain, with ruff starched clean and furred cap that smelt faintly of winter storage and city streets. With him came a different sound into the house: the faint jingle of his chain when he moved, the firmer step of a man risen in the world. He was received not with affection only, but with respect; in those days such steps upward were counted almost as clearly as those in a stair.

When he had been admitted to the council, and the matter told, his face showed plainly—though he kept his voice civil—that his pride was wounded by their having deigned to treat with Margaret Brandt at all.

“I see the temptation,” said he. “But which of us hath not at times to wish one way and do another?”

It cast a chill on the old folk; the room’s earlier warmth went thin, as if a door had opened to a draught. Little Kate, quick to mend the broken harmony of voices as a careful hand mends a torn cloth, spoke softly:

“Vex not thyself, dear Richart. Mother says she will not come.”

“All the better, sweetheart,” said he. “I fear me, if she do, I shall hie me back to Amsterdam.”

At that instant Denys popped his head in at the door—his entrance brisk as a ladle tapping the pot to say it is time.

“She will be here at three on the great dial,” said he.

They all looked at one another in silence, while outside the day went on with its ordinary sounds—the distant call in the street, the wind against the shutters—each noise a reminder that the world does not pause for any family’s bitterness, nor even for the taste of a son’s far-off words.
